chapters.title: Flee from Sin as from a Snake
chapters.html:
Sirach 21

1My child, have you sinned? Do not do it again,
and pray about your former sins.

2Flee from sin as from a snake;
for if you go near it, it will bite you.
Its teeth are a lion's teeth,
destroying the souls of men.

3All lawlessness is like a two-edged sword;
there is no healing for its wound.

4Terror and violence will lay waste wealth;
so the house of the proud will be laid waste.

5The prayer of a poor man goes from his mouth to His ears,
and His judgment comes quickly.

6Whoever hates reproof walks in the steps of a sinner,
but he who fears the Lord will turn back in his heart.

7The man mighty in speech is known far and wide,
but the man of understanding knows when he slips.

8Whoever builds his house with other people's money
is like one who gathers his stones for the winter.

9An assembly of the lawless is tow gathered together,
and their end is a flame of fire.

10The way of sinners is smoothly paved with stones,
but at its end is the pit of Hades.

11Whoever keeps the law masters his thoughts,
and the fulfillment of the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

12One who is not shrewd cannot be taught,
but there is a shrewdness that multiplies bitterness.

13The knowledge of a wise man will increase like a flood,
and his counsel like a fountain of life.

14The inside of a fool is like a broken jar;
it will hold no knowledge.

15When a man of knowledge hears a wise saying,
he will praise it and add to it;
when a self-indulgent man hears it, it displeases him,
and he throws it behind his back.

16A fool's talk is like a burden on a journey,
but grace will be found on the lips of the intelligent.

17The mouth of a sensible man will be sought in the assembly,
and they will ponder his words in their heart.

18Like a house in ruins is wisdom to a fool,
and the knowledge of the senseless is talk without sense.

19To the senseless, discipline is fetters on the feet,
and like handcuffs on the right hand.

20A fool raises his voice when he laughs,
but a shrewd man will barely smile, and quietly.

21To a sensible man discipline is like a golden ornament,
and like a bracelet on the right arm.

22The foot of a fool is quick to enter a house,
but a man of experience holds back out of respect.

23A foolish man peers into the house from the door,
but a well-taught man will stand outside.

24It is bad manners for a man to listen at a door,
and the sensible man would be weighed down by the disgrace.

25The lips of strangers will be heavy with these things,
but the words of the sensible will be weighed in the balance.

26The heart of fools is in their mouth,
but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.

27When the ungodly man curses the adversary,
he curses his own soul.

28The whisperer defiles his own soul,
and is hated wherever he lives.

Notes

  • v1 "have you sinned? Do not do it again" — compare Jesus to the woman: go, and from now on sin no more (John 8:11).

  • v3 "a two-edged sword" — rhomphaia distomos, the sword that Revelation sees coming from the mouth of the Son of Man (Revelation 1:16); here, the wound sin leaves.

  • v5 "from his mouth to His ears" — the poor man's prayer goes straight to God (Exodus 22:23).

  • v8 "for the winter" — eis cheimōna, as Swete prints it; the line is obscure: perhaps stones gathered in a season when no one can build.

  • v9 "tow" — the fiber of flax, which flares up and is gone (Isaiah 1:31).

  • v10 "smoothly paved… the pit of Hades" — compare Proverbs 14:12, there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the ways of death, and the broad way of Matthew 7:13.

  • v15 "a self-indulgent man" — spatalōn, the word Paul uses of the widow who is self-indulgent (1 Timothy 5:6).

  • vv22–24 — manners at a door, the reverse of the seeker of 14:23 who peers in at wisdom's window.

  • v27 "When the ungodly man curses the adversary" — ton satanan, "the adversary" or "Satan": he blames the devil, or his own opponent, and the curse falls on himself, since the enemy is within. The Greek uses the same word for the accuser of Job 1–2.

chapters.title: The Fool and the Friend
chapters.html:
Sirach 22

1The sluggard is like a filthy stone,
and everyone hisses at his disgrace.

2The sluggard is like a lump of dung;
anyone who picks it up shakes it off his hand.

3It is a father's disgrace to have fathered an undisciplined son,
and a daughter is born to his loss.

4A sensible daughter will gain a husband of her own,
but one who brings shame is a grief to her father.

5A bold daughter brings shame on father and husband,
and will be despised by both.

6Like music in mourning is a story told at the wrong time,
but whips and discipline are wisdom at every time.

7Whoever teaches a fool glues potsherds together,
or rouses a sleeper from deep sleep.

8Whoever tells a story to a fool tells it to a man half asleep,
and at the end he will say, "What is it?"

9(This verse is not in the Greek text followed here; see the note.)

10(This verse is not in the Greek text followed here; see the note.)

11Weep for the dead, for he has lost the light;
and weep for the fool, for he has lost understanding.
Weep less bitterly for the dead, for he has found rest;
but the life of the fool is worse than death.

12Mourning for the dead lasts seven days,
but for a fool and an ungodly man, all the days of his life.

13Do not talk much with a fool,
and do not visit a senseless man;
guard yourself from him, so that you may not have trouble,
nor be spattered when he shakes himself;
turn away from him and you will find rest,
and you will not be worn out by his madness.

14What is heavier than lead?
What is its name but "Fool"?

15Sand and salt and a lump of iron
are easier to bear than a senseless man.

16Timber bound firmly into a building
will not come loose in an earthquake;
so a heart set firm on a well-considered plan
will not be afraid in a crisis.

17A heart fixed on sensible thinking
is like the sanded plaster on a smooth wall.

18Stakes set on a height
will not stand against the wind;
so a timid heart with a fool's thoughts
will not stand against any fear.

19Whoever pricks the eye brings tears,
and whoever pricks the heart brings feelings to light.

20One who throws a stone at birds scares them away,
and one who reviles a friend breaks off the friendship.

21If you have drawn a sword against a friend,
do not despair, for there is a way back.

22If you have opened your mouth against a friend,
do not worry, for there can be reconciliation;
but reviling, arrogance, the telling of a secret, and a treacherous blow —
from these any friend will flee.

23Win your neighbor's trust in his poverty,
so that you may share in his good things with him;
stand by him in time of trouble,
so that you may share his inheritance with him.

24Before the fire come the vapor and smoke of the furnace;
so before bloodshed come insults.

25I will not be ashamed to shelter a friend,
and I will not hide from him;

26and if harm comes to me because of him,
everyone who hears of it will beware of him.

27Who will set a guard over my mouth,
and a shrewd seal upon my lips,
so that I may not fall because of them,
and my tongue may not destroy me?

  • vv1–2 — the sluggard, as in Proverbs 6:6–11 and 24:30–34, here in two pictures nobody wants to touch.

  • vv3–5 — the line as it stands calls the birth of a daughter a loss to her father; vv4–5 then set the sensible daughter, who gains a husband, beside the bold one, who shames both father and husband.

  • v6 "Like music in mourning" — compare Reproof 1:20 (Proverbs 25:20), is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.

  • vv9–10 — Swete's Greek gives these verse numbers and no words (see the note on 1:5).

  • v12 "Mourning for the dead lasts seven days" — as Joseph made mourning for his father seven days (Genesis 50:10).

  • v13 "nor be spattered when he shakes himself" — entinagmos, a shaking off, as a wet animal shakes itself over those nearby.

  • v15 "Sand and salt and a lump of iron are easier to bear" — Reproof 3:3 (Proverbs 27:3), A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's vexation is heavier than both.

  • v22 "the telling of a secret" — Reproof 1:9 (Proverbs 25:9), do not reveal another's secret.

  • v27 "Who will set a guard over my mouth" — Psalm 141:3, Set a guard, LORD, over my mouth. The question opens a prayer that runs into the next chapter.

chapters.title: Discipline of the Mouth
chapters.html:
Sirach 23

1Lord, Father and Master of my life,
do not abandon me to their counsel;
do not let me fall by them.

2Who will set whips over my thoughts,
and the discipline of wisdom over my heart,
so that they may not spare me for my errors,
and my sins may not pass unnoticed,

3so that my errors may not multiply,
and my sins abound,
and I fall before my adversaries,
and my enemy rejoice over me?

4Lord, Father and God of my life,
do not give me haughty eyes,

5and turn desire away from me;

6let neither gluttony nor lust take hold of me,
and do not give me over to a shameless soul.

7Discipline of the mouth.
Listen, children, to the discipline of the mouth;
whoever keeps it will never be caught.
By his own lips

8the sinner will be overtaken,
the reviler and the proud will stumble by them.

9Do not accustom your mouth to oaths,
nor make a habit of naming the Holy One.

10For as a servant who is constantly examined
will not be without bruises,
so also the man who always swears and names the Holy One
will not be cleansed from sin.

11A man who swears many oaths will be filled with lawlessness,
and the scourge will not leave his house;
if he offends, his sin remains on him,
and if he disregards it, he has sinned twice;

14Remember your father and mother

and you will curse the day of your birth.

15A man accustomed to abusive words

and a third brings on wrath:

who will not stop until the fire burns him up.

17To the man who commits fornication all bread is sweet;

Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me,
and no one sees me. Why should I fear?

and he does not know that the eyes of the Lord

looking upon all the ways of men

and so it is after they were finished.

second, she has offended against her husband;
and third, she has committed adultery through fornication

24She will be brought out before the assembly,
and her children will be called to account.

25Her children will not spread their roots,
and her branches will bear no fruit.

  • v7 "Discipline of the mouth." — a heading written into the Greek text, as at 18:30 and 20:26.

  • vv9–11 "Do not accustom your mouth to oaths" — the third commandment, You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain (Exodus 20:7); compare Jesus, Do not swear at all (Matthew 5:34).

  • v12 "a way of speaking that is clothed in death" — blasphemy, for which the Law set the penalty of death (Leviticus 24:16).

  • v14 "you will curse the day of your birth" — as Job did (Job 3:1–3).

chapters.title: The Praise of Wisdom
chapters.html:
Sirach 24

1The praise of wisdom.
Wisdom will praise herself,
and will glory among her people.

2In the assembly of the Most High she will open her mouth,
and before His host she will glory:

3"I came out of the mouth of the Most High,
and covered the earth like a mist.

4I dwelt in the heights,
and my throne was in a pillar of cloud.

5Alone I went around the circle of heaven,
and walked in the depths of the abyss.

6Over the waves of the sea, and over all the earth,
and over every people and nation I have held sway.

7Among all these I sought a resting place;
in whose inheritance should I lodge?

8Then the Creator of all things gave me a command,
and He who created me gave my tent a resting place,
and said, 'Pitch your tent in Jacob,
and receive your inheritance in Israel.'

9Before the ages, from the beginning, He created me,
and to the ages I shall not cease.

10In the holy tent I ministered before Him,
and so I was established in Zion.

11In the beloved city likewise He gave me rest,
and in Jerusalem was my authority.

12I took root among an honored people,
in the portion of the Lord, His inheritance.

13I grew tall like a cedar in Lebanon,
and like a cypress on the mountains of Hermon.

14I grew tall like a palm tree on the shores,
and like rose bushes in Jericho;
like a fair olive tree in the plain,
and I grew tall like a plane tree.

15Like cinnamon and camel's thorn I gave forth the scent of spices,
and like choice myrrh I spread a sweet fragrance,
like galbanum and onycha and stacte,
and like the smoke of frankincense in the tent.

16Like a terebinth I spread out my branches,
and my branches are branches of glory and grace.

17Like a vine I put forth grace,
and my blossoms became the fruit of glory and wealth.

18(This verse is not in the Greek text followed here; see the note.)

19Come to me, you who desire me,
and eat your fill of my fruits.

20For the memory of me is sweeter than honey,
and my inheritance sweeter than the honeycomb.

21Those who eat me will hunger for more,
and those who drink me will thirst for more.

22Whoever obeys me will not be put to shame,
and those who work with me will not sin."

23All these things are the book of the covenant of the Most High God,
the law that Moses commanded,
an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob.

24(This verse is not in the Greek text followed here; see the note.)

25It fills men with wisdom like the Pishon,
and like the Tigris in the days of first fruits;

26it makes understanding overflow like the Euphrates,
and like the Jordan in the days of harvest;

27it makes discipline shine like the light,
like the Gihon in the days of vintage.

28The first man did not know her fully,
nor will the last trace her out;

29for her thought is fuller than the sea,
and her counsel deeper than the great abyss.

30As for me, I came out like a canal from a river,
and like a water channel into a garden.

31I said, "I will water my garden,
and drench my flower bed";
and my canal became a river,
and my river became a sea.

32I will again make discipline shine like the dawn,
and make it shine far and wide.

33I will again pour out teaching like prophecy,
and leave it to all future generations.

34See that I have not labored for myself alone,
but for all who seek her.

Notes

  • v1 "The praise of wisdom." — a heading written into the Greek text. The chapter stands at the center of the book: wisdom speaks in her own voice, as in Proverbs 8, and is found to be the Law given to Israel (v23).

  • v3 "I came out of the mouth of the Most High" — wisdom as God's spoken word: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made (Psalm 33:6).

  • vv4, 8 "I dwelt… Pitch your tent in Jacob" — kataskēnoun, "to pitch a tent," the word of God's dwelling in the tabernacle; John uses the same verb of the Word: the Word became flesh and pitched His tent among us (John 1:14, eskēnōsen). "A pillar of cloud" — the cloud that led Israel (Exodus 13:21).

  • v9 "Before the ages, from the beginning, He created me" — the Greek of Proverbs 8:22–23, as at 1:4.

  • v12 "the portion of the Lord" — Israel, as in 17:17 and Deuteronomy 32:9.

  • v15 "galbanum and onycha and stacte… frankincense in the tent" — the spices of the holy incense (Exodus 30:34) and, with cinnamon, of the anointing oil (30:23): wisdom is the fragrance of the sanctuary.

  • v18, v24 — Swete's Greek gives these verse numbers and no words (see the note on 1:5).

  • vv19–21 "Come to me… Those who eat me will hunger for more" — wisdom's invitation, as in Proverbs 9:5. Jesus says the opposite of Himself: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to Me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

  • v23 "the law that Moses commanded, an inheritance for the assemblies of Jacob" — almost word for word the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:4 (nomon hon eneteilato… Mōusēs, klēronomian synagōgais Iakōb); the Hebrew there reads Moses commanded us an instruction, a possession for the assembly of Jacob. Here the Law and wisdom are one.

  • vv25–27 "the Pishon… the Tigris… the Euphrates… the Gihon" — the rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:10–14), with the Jordan, which overflows all its banks all the days of harvest (Joshua 3:15): the Law overflows with wisdom like the rivers of paradise. In vv30–31 the teacher's own small channel grows into a river and a sea.

chapters.title: Nine Things and a Tenth
chapters.html:
Sirach 25

1In three things I am made beautiful,
and stand in beauty before the Lord and men:
harmony among brothers, friendship among neighbors,
and a wife and husband who suit each other.

2My soul hates three kinds of men,
and I am greatly offended by their life:
a proud poor man, a lying rich man,
and an old adulterer lacking in sense.

3If you have gathered nothing in your youth,
how can you find anything in your old age?

4How fitting is judgment for gray hairs,
and for elders to know good counsel!

5How fitting is wisdom in the aged,
and understanding and counsel in men of honor!

6Rich experience is the crown of the aged,
and their boast is the fear of the Lord.

7Nine things I have thought of and called blessed in my heart,
and a tenth I will tell with my tongue:
a man who rejoices in his children;
a man who lives to see the fall of his enemies;

8happy is he who lives with a sensible wife,
and he who has not slipped with his tongue,
and he who has not served a man unworthy of him;

9happy is he who has found prudence,
and he who speaks to listening ears;

10how great is he who has found wisdom!
But there is none above him who fears the Lord.

11The fear of the Lord surpasses everything;
to whom shall the one who holds it be compared?

12(This verse is not in the Greek text followed here; see the note.)

13Any wound, but not a wound of the heart!
Any wickedness, but not the wickedness of a wife!

14Any attack, but not an attack from those who hate!
Any vengeance, but not the vengeance of enemies!

15There is no head above the head of a snake,
and no anger above the anger of an enemy.

16I would rather live with a lion and a dragon
than live with an evil wife.

17The wickedness of a wife changes her appearance,
and darkens her face like sackcloth.

18Her husband sits among his neighbors,
and when he hears it, he sighs bitterly.

19Any wickedness is small beside the wickedness of a wife;
may a sinner's lot fall upon her!

20A sandy ascent for the feet of the aged —
such is a talkative wife to a quiet husband.

21Do not fall for a woman's beauty,
and do not set your desire on a woman.

22There is anger and impudence and great disgrace
when a wife provides for her husband.

23A dejected heart and a gloomy face
and a wounded heart come from an evil wife;
drooping hands and weak knees
from a wife who does not make her husband happy.

24From a woman sin had its beginning,
and because of her we all die.

25Do not give water an outlet,
nor an evil wife free rein.

26If she does not go as you direct,
cut her off from your flesh.

Notes

  • vv1–2, 7–11 "In three things… three kinds of men… Nine things… and a tenth" — the counting sayings of Reproof 6 (Proverbs 30), here three good things, three hateful men, and ten blessings, the tenth and highest the fear of the Lord.

  • v12 — Swete's Greek gives this verse number and no words (see the note on 1:5).

  • vv13–26 — the evil wife, a long passage that 26:1–4 and 26:13–18 answer with the good wife, as Proverbs closes with the capable wife (Reproof 7:10–31).

  • v15 "no head above the head of a snake" — the snake's head is where its venom is; nothing strikes worse.

  • v22 "when a wife provides for her husband" — epichorēgē, "supplies": a husband kept by his wife's wealth.

  • v24 "From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die" — Genesis 3:6. Paul tells the same story through the man: through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin (Romans 5:12).

  • v26 "cut her off from your flesh" — divorce, the undoing of the "one flesh" of Genesis 2:24 (Deuteronomy 24:1).

chapters.title: A Good Wife
chapters.html:
Sirach 26

1Happy is the husband of a good wife;
the number of his days will be doubled.

2A capable wife gladdens her husband,
and he will complete his years in peace.

3A good wife is a good portion;
she will be given as a portion to those who fear the Lord.

4Whether rich or poor, his heart is glad,
and his face is always cheerful.

5Of three things my heart is afraid,
and over a fourth I have pleaded:
the slander of a city, the gathering of a mob,
and false accusation — all these are worse than death.

6A wife jealous of another wife is grief of heart and sorrow,
and a scourge of the tongue that shares it with all.

7An evil wife is an ox yoke that slips;
whoever takes hold of her is like one who grasps a scorpion.

8A drunken wife arouses great anger;
she will not hide her shame.

9A wife's unchastity shows in her bold glances,
and is known by her eyelids.

10Over a daughter keep a firm and unyielding watch,
or, finding freedom, she will use it for herself.

11Be on guard against an impudent eye,
and do not be surprised if she wrongs you;

12as a thirsty traveler opens his mouth
and drinks from any water near him,
so she will sit in front of every tent peg
and open her quiver to the arrow.

13A wife's charm delights her husband,
and her skill puts fat on his bones.

14A silent wife is a gift of the Lord,
and nothing can be given in exchange for a well-disciplined soul.

15A modest wife adds grace upon grace,
and no scale can weigh the worth of a self-controlled soul.

16Like the sun rising in the heights of the Lord,
so is the beauty of a good wife in his well-ordered home.

17Like the lamp shining on the holy lampstand,
so is the beauty of a face on a stately figure.

18Like golden pillars on a base of silver,
so are shapely feet with a steady heart.

and at a third anger comes over me:

and men of understanding treated as refuse;

the Lord will prepare him for the sword.

29A merchant can hardly keep himself from wrongdoing,
and a tradesman will not be declared innocent of sin.

  • v2 "A capable wife" — gynē andreia, the "capable wife" whom Proverbs praises at its close (Reproof 7:10; Proverbs 31:10).

  • vv5–6 "Of three things my heart is afraid, and over a fourth I have pleaded" — the fourth is v6, a wife set against a rival wife in the same house, as Peninnah provoked Hannah (Her rival used to provoke her severely, 1 Samuel 1:6). "I have pleaded" — edeēthēn, as Swete prints it.

  • vv10–12 — counsel to a father, put in plain pictures; the subject is taken up again in 42:9–11.

  • vv16–18 "Like the sun… like the lamp on the holy lampstand… like golden pillars on a base of silver" — the good wife's beauty likened to the sanctuary: the lampstand (Exodus 25:31–37) and the pillars overlaid with gold on sockets of silver (Exodus 26:32).

  • v18 "with a steady heart" — epi sternois, "on the chest" of one who stands firm, as Swete prints it.

  • vv19–27 — Swete's Greek gives these nine verse numbers and no words (see the note on 1:5).

  • v28 "treated as refuse" — skybalisthōsin, from skybalon, "refuse," the word Paul uses of all he gave up for Christ (Philippians 3:8).

chapters.title: Speech Reveals the Man

Sirach 27

1Many have sinned for a trifle,
and whoever seeks to grow rich will turn his eye away.

2As a stake is driven fast between the joints of stones,
so sin is wedged in between selling and buying.

3If a man does not hold fast to the fear of the Lord with zeal,
his house will soon be overthrown.

4When a sieve is shaken, the refuse remains;
so a man's faults remain in his reasoning.

5The kiln tests the potter's vessels,
and the test of a man is in his reasoning.

6The fruit shows how a tree has been tended;
so a man's speech shows the thought of his heart.

7Do not praise a man before you hear him reason,
for this is the test of men.

8If you pursue justice, you will attain it,
and put it on like a glorious long robe.

9Birds roost with their own kind,
and truth returns to those who practice it.

chapters.title: Forgive Your Neighbor
chapters.html:
Sirach 28

1Whoever takes vengeance will meet vengeance from the Lord,
and He will keep strict account of his sins.

2Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done,
and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven.

3Does a man harbor anger against another,
and yet seek healing from the Lord?

4Does he show no mercy to a man like himself,
and yet pray about his own sins?

5If he, being flesh, keeps up his wrath,
who will make atonement for his sins?

6Remember the end of your life, and stop hating;
remember decay and death, and keep to the commandments.

7Remember the commandments, and do not be angry with your neighbor;
remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook ignorance.

8Keep away from strife, and you will lessen sins;
for a hot-tempered man kindles strife,

9and a sinful man stirs up trouble among friends,
and sows slander among those at peace.

10As the fuel is, so the fire will burn;
as a man's strength is, so will his anger be;
as his wealth is, so will his wrath rise;
and as the strife is stubborn, so will it blaze.

11A hasty quarrel kindles a fire,
and urgent strife sheds blood.

12If you blow on a spark, it will blaze;
if you spit on it, it will be put out;
and both come out of your mouth.

13Curse the whisperer and the double-tongued,
for they have destroyed many who were at peace.

14A third tongue has shaken many,
and scattered them from nation to nation;
it has torn down strong cities,
and overturned the houses of great men.

15A third tongue has driven out capable wives,
and robbed them of the fruit of their labors.

16Whoever listens to it will find no rest,
nor will he settle down in peace.

17The blow of a whip raises a welt,
but the blow of the tongue breaks bones.

18Many have fallen by the sword,
but not so many as have fallen because of the tongue.

19Happy is the man who is sheltered from it,
who has not gone through its wrath,
who has not borne its yoke,
and has not been bound with its fetters;

20for its yoke is a yoke of iron,
and its fetters are fetters of bronze;

21its death is an evil death,
and Hades is better than it.

22It will not rule over the godly,
and they will not be burned in its flame.

23Those who forsake the Lord will fall into its power;
it will burn among them and not be put out;
it will be sent out against them like a lion,
and like a leopard it will tear them.

24Fence your property with thorns;
lock up your silver and gold;

25make a balance and a weight for your words,
and a door and a bolt for your mouth.

26Take care not to slip by it,
or you may fall before one who lies in wait.

Notes

  • v1 "Whoever takes vengeance will meet vengeance from the Lord" — Vengeance is Mine, and recompense (Deuteronomy 32:35), which Paul quotes (Romans 12:19). "He will keep strict account" — diastēriōn diastērisei, the verb doubled for force.

  • vv2–5 "Forgive your neighbor… and then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven" — the teaching of the Lord's Prayer, forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors (Matthew 6:12, 14–15), and of the servant forgiven much who would not forgive little (18:23–35).

  • v7 "do not be angry with your neighbor" — You shall not take revenge and you shall not hold a grudge… you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

  • v8 "a hot-tempered man kindles strife" — Proverbs 15:18, A hot-tempered man stirs up strife.

  • v12 "both come out of your mouth" — the same mouth fans the spark or puts it out: from the same mouth come blessing and cursing (James 3:10).

  • vv14–15 "A third tongue" — glōssa tritē, the slanderer who comes between two people and destroys them both. "Capable wives" — gynaikas andreias, as in 26:2.

  • v17 "the blow of the tongue breaks bones" — compare Reproof 1:15 (Proverbs 25:15), a soft tongue will break a bone, where gentleness is the strength; here, malice.

  • v20 "a yoke of iron" — as Jeremiah was told, you have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron (Jeremiah 28:13).

  • vv24–25 "a door and a bolt for your mouth" — the prayer of 22:27 and Psalm 141:3, Set a guard, LORD, over my mouth. "Fence your property" — ide, "see," cut.

chapters.title: Lend to Your Neighbor
chapters.html:
Sirach 29

1Whoever shows mercy will lend to his neighbor,
and whoever strengthens him with his hand keeps the commandments.

2Lend to your neighbor in the time of his need,
and in turn repay your neighbor on time.

3Keep your word and keep faith with him,
and at all times you will find what you need.

4Many have treated a loan as a windfall,
and have brought trouble on those who helped them.

5Until he gets it, he will kiss the lender's hand,
and speak humbly about his neighbor's money;
but when it is time to repay, he will drag out the time,
repay with words of indifference,
and blame the times.

6If the lender prevails, he will hardly get back half,
and will count that a windfall;
if not, he has been robbed of his money,
and has made an enemy at his own cost,
who will repay him with curses and abuse,
and instead of honor will repay him with dishonor.

7Because of wickedness many have refused to lend;
they were afraid of being robbed for nothing.

8Yet be patient with a man in humble circumstances,
and for charity's sake give him time.

9For the commandment's sake help the poor man,
and in his need do not send him away empty.

10Lose your silver for a brother and a friend,
and do not let it rust under a stone and be lost.

11Lay up your treasure by the commandments of the Most High,
and it will profit you more than gold.

12Store up charity in your storerooms,
and it will rescue you from every harm;

13better than a mighty shield and a strong spear,
it will fight for you against the enemy.

14A good man will stand surety for his neighbor,
but one who has lost all shame will abandon him.

15Do not forget the kindness of your surety,
for he has given his life for you.

16A sinner will ruin the goods of his surety,

17and one ungrateful at heart will abandon his rescuer.

18Surety has ruined many who were prospering,
and tossed them like a wave of the sea;
it has driven powerful men from their homes,
and they have wandered among foreign nations.

19A sinner who falls into surety
and chases profit from contracts will fall into lawsuits.

20Help your neighbor as far as you are able,
and take care that you do not fall yourself.

21The first needs of life are water and bread and clothing,
and a house to cover one's nakedness.

22Better is a poor man's life under a shelter of logs
than splendid food in other men's houses.

23Be content with little or much.

24It is a miserable life to go from house to house;
where a man lives as a guest, he will not open his mouth.

25You will entertain and pour drinks and get no thanks,
and on top of this you will hear bitter words:

26"Come here, guest, set the table;
if you have anything in your hand, give it to me to eat."

27"Out, guest, make way for someone of honor;
my brother has come to stay with me; I need the room."

28These things are hard for a man of understanding:
reproach over his lodging, and the insults of a moneylender.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "Whoever shows mercy will lend to his neighbor" — lending as an act of mercy, as the law commands it: Rather, you shall open, open your hand to him, and lend, lend him enough for his need (Deuteronomy 15:8). Jesus: do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you (Matthew 5:42).

  • vv5–6 "repay with words of indifference" — apodōsei, the verb of v2, repay your neighbor on time. What this borrower repays is words, then curses, then dishonor (v6, the same verb twice).

  • v8 "for charity's sake give him time" — ep' eleēmosynēn parelkyseis auton, "you will draw him out toward charity." Swete prints no "not." The verb means to drag out or put off; set beside be patient in the line before, it is the lender giving a poor man more time and counting the delay as charity.

  • v11 "Lay up your treasure" — Tobit 4:9, storing up a good treasure for yourself against the day of need; and Jesus, store up for yourselves treasures in heaven (Matthew 6:20).

  • v15 "he has given his life for you" — edōken tēn psychēn autou hyper sou: the surety pledges himself in the debtor's place. Jesus uses the same words of Himself, to give His life as a ransom for many (dounai tēn psychēn autou, Mark 10:45).

  • vv14–20 — surety again: Proverbs warns against it altogether (6:1–5); Sirach allows it within one's means (8:13), and here, as far as you are able (v20).

  • vv24–27 "where a man lives as a guest" — paroikēsei, and paroike, "guest," twice in the host's two speeches: the man with no house of his own must set the table, and then give up his room.

  • v28 "the insults of a moneylender" — the chapter ends where it began, with lending.

chapters.title: Concerning Children
chapters.html:
Sirach 30

1Concerning children.
Whoever loves his son will whip him often,
so that he may rejoice in him at the last.

2Whoever disciplines his son will profit from him,
and will boast of him among his acquaintances.

3Whoever teaches his son will make his enemy jealous,
and will rejoice in him before his friends.

4When his father dies, it is as though he had not died,
for he has left behind him one like himself.

5In his life he saw him and rejoiced,
and at his death he did not grieve;

6he has left behind an avenger against his enemies,
and one to repay kindness to his friends.

7For his sons' lives he will bind up his wounds,
and at every cry his heart will be shaken.

8An unbroken horse turns out stubborn,
and a son left to himself turns out headstrong.

9Pamper a child, and he will terrify you;
play with him, and he will grieve you.

10Do not laugh with him, or you will grieve with him,
and in the end you will grind your teeth.

11Do not give him free rein in his youth;

12bruise his ribs while he is a child,
or he will grow stubborn and disobey you.

13Discipline your son and take pains with him,
so that he does not stumble, to your disgrace.

14Better a poor man who is healthy and strong in body
than a rich man plagued in his body.

15Health and soundness are better than any gold,
and a strong body than boundless wealth.

16Concerning food.
There is no wealth better than health of body,
and no gladness above joy of heart.

17Death is better than a bitter life,
or a lasting illness.

18Good things poured out on a closed mouth
are like offerings of food set by a grave.

19What good is an offering to an idol?
It can neither eat nor smell.
So is the man who is hounded by the Lord:

20he sees with his eyes and groans,
like a eunuch who embraces a virgin and groans.

21Do not give yourself over to sorrow,
and do not distress yourself with your own thoughts.

22Gladness of heart is the life of a man,
and a man's joy is length of days.

23Love your soul and comfort your heart,
and drive sorrow far from you;
for sorrow has killed many,
and there is no profit in it.

24Envy and anger shorten one's days,
and anxiety brings old age before its time.

25A cheerful and good heart
attends to the food it eats.

Notes

  • v1 "Concerning children" — a heading in the Greek text, as at v16, Concerning food. "Will whip him often" — endelechēsei mastigas autō, "will keep up lashes on him": Proverbs 13:24, Whoever spares his rod hates his son.

  • vv4–6 "it is as though he had not died, for he has left behind him one like himself" — the son who carries on his father: he avenges his father's enemies and repays his father's friends.

  • v7 "For his sons' lives he will bind up his wounds" — peri psychōn huiōn katadesmeusei traumata autou, as Swete prints it: the father's anxiety for his sons, set between the son who carries on his father (vv4–6) and the son left to himself (vv8–13).

  • v18 "offerings of food set by a grave" — food laid at a tomb for the dead, who cannot eat it. Tobit 4:17 commands the custom as charity, Pour out your bread on the grave of the righteous; here it is the picture of good things wasted on a man who can no longer taste them.

  • v19 "It can neither eat nor smell" — the idols of Deuteronomy 4:28, which neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell, and Psalm 115:6, noses, but do not smell. "Hounded by the Lord" — ekdiōkomenos, "driven out, pursued": the sick man who cannot eat the good things set before him.

  • v20 "like a eunuch who embraces a virgin" — the image of 20:4, where it stands for justice done by force; here it is the sick man who holds good things and cannot enjoy them.

  • v23 "Love your soul" — agapa tēn psychēn sou: care for your own life, the opposite of the sorrow that has killed many.

  • v25 — Swete prints this line at the end of v24. From here to chapter 36 the Greek text Swete prints has two blocks of chapters in exchanged order, and Swete numbers them as they stand: his 30:25–40 is English 33:16–31, his 31–33 are English 34:1–36:11, his 34–35 are English 31–32, and his 36 is English 33:1–16 with 36:11–26. The English numbering is followed.

chapters.title: Gold, the Table and Wine
chapters.html:
Sirach 31

1Lying awake over wealth wastes away the flesh,
and the anxiety it brings drives away sleep.

2Wakeful anxiety keeps slumber away,
and a grave illness drives off sleep.

3The rich man toils to gather money,
and when he rests he fills himself with his delicacies.

4The poor man toils on a meager living,
and when he rests he is in want.

5Whoever loves gold will not be declared righteous,
and whoever pursues ruin will have his fill of it.

6Many have been brought to their fall because of gold,
and their destruction met them face to face.

7It is a stumbling block to those who worship it,
and every fool will be caught by it.

8Happy is the rich man who is found without blemish,
and who has not gone after gold.

9Who is he? We will call him happy,
for he has done wonders among his people.

10Who has been tested by it and found perfect?
Let that be his boast.
Who could have transgressed and did not transgress,
and could have done evil and did not do it?

11His goods will be made secure,
and the assembly will tell of his acts of charity.

12Are you seated at a great table?
Do not open your throat over it,
and do not say, "How much there is on it!"

13Remember that an evil eye is a bad thing.
What has been created more evil than the eye?
That is why it weeps at everything.

14Where he looks, do not reach out your hand,
and do not crowd him at the dish.

15Judge your neighbor's feelings by your own,
and be thoughtful in everything.

16Eat what is set before you as a human being should,
and do not gobble, or you will be hated.

17Be the first to stop, for discipline's sake,
and do not be greedy, or you will give offense.

18If you sit among many,
do not reach out your hand before they do.

19How little is enough for a well-disciplined man!
On his bed he does not gasp for breath.

20Healthy sleep comes with a moderate stomach;
he rises early and has his wits about him.
Sleeplessness and vomiting and colic
are with the greedy man.

21If you have been pressed to eat too much,
get up and leave in the middle, and you will have relief.

22Listen to me, my child, and do not despise me,

24The city will grumble at a man who is stingy with food,

25Do not play the hero over wine,

26As the furnace tests the temper of steel in the quenching,

27Wine is as good as life to men,

29Wine drunk to excess is bitterness of soul,

30Drunkenness increases a fool's rage until he stumbles,

  • v7 "those who worship it" — enthysiazousin, as Swete prints it. Spelled so, the word is built on thysia, "sacrifice": those who sacrifice to it. Spelled enthousiazousin, it is those possessed by it, as by a god. Either way gold has become an idol.

  • vv8–10 "Who could have transgressed and did not transgress" — the rich man without blemish (amōmos) is praised for the wrong he had the means to do and did not do.

chapters.title: At the Banquet
chapters.html:
Sirach 32

1Have they made you master of the feast? Do not exalt yourself;
be among them as one of them;
look after them, and then take your seat.

2When you have done all your duty, recline,
so that you may be glad because of them,
and receive a crown for your good conduct.

3Speak, elder, for it is fitting for you,
but with exact knowledge,
and do not interrupt the music.

4Where there is a performance, do not pour out talk,
and do not show off your wisdom at the wrong time.

5A seal of ruby in a setting of gold
is a concert of music at a banquet of wine.

6A seal of emerald in a work of gold
is the melody of music with pleasant wine.

7Speak, young man, if you are needed,
but scarcely twice, and only if you are asked.

8Sum up what you say, much in few words;
be like one who knows and yet keeps silent.

9Among the great do not make yourself their equal,
and when another is speaking, do not chatter on.

10Lightning hurries ahead of thunder,
and favor goes ahead of a modest man.

11Rise at the right time and do not be the last;
hurry home and do not linger.

12There amuse yourself and do what you have in mind,
but do not sin with a proud word.

13For all this, bless Him who made you
and who gives you your fill of His good things.

14Whoever fears the Lord will accept discipline,
and those who rise early will find favor.

15Whoever seeks the law will be filled with it,
but the hypocrite will stumble over it.

16Those who fear the Lord will find what is right,
and will kindle righteous deeds like a light.

17A sinful man turns aside from reproof,
and finds a ruling to suit his own will.

18A man of counsel will not overlook a thought;
the stranger and the proud man do not shrink in fear,
even after acting without counsel.

19Do nothing without counsel,
and when you have acted, do not regret it.

20Do not walk on a road of stumbling,
and do not trip among the stones.

21Do not trust a smooth road,

22and guard yourself against your own children.

23In every work trust your own soul,
for this too is keeping the commandments.

24Whoever trusts the law pays attention to the commandments,
and whoever relies on the Lord will suffer no loss.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "master of the feast… receive a crown" — hēgoumenon, the one chosen to preside over a banquet, who sees to the guests before he takes his own place; the crown is the garland worn at a feast (Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds, Wisdom 2:8), here given for eukosmia, good order.

  • vv5–6 "A seal of ruby… a seal of emerald" — a signet stone set in gold: music is the jewel in the setting of the feast.

  • v10 "a modest man" — aischyntērou, the word of 26:15, where a modest wife adds grace upon grace; here too modesty wins favor before a word is said.

  • v13 "gives you your fill" — methyskonta, "making you drunk," the banquet's own word turned to God's gifts. The Greek of Psalm 36:8 uses it the same way: They are filled with the abundance of Your house (methysthēsontai).

  • v14 "those who rise early" — to seek the Lord, as those who rise early for wisdom in 4:12, those who rise early for her will be filled with joy.

  • v15 "the hypocrite" — ho hypokrinomenos, "the one playing a part," an actor's word; from the same verb comes the noun Jesus uses, hypokritai, "hypocrites" (Matthew 6:2).

  • v18 "even after acting without counsel" — kai meta to poiēsai met' autou aneu boulēs, "and after doing with him without counsel": the line is that compressed in the Greek.

  • v22 "guard yourself against your own children" — apo tōn teknōn sou phylaxai, as Swete prints it.

  • vv21–24 "Do not trust… trust your own soul… Whoever trusts the law" — pisteuō three times: not the smooth road, but your own soul and the law. The last line turns to a second verb, pepoithōs, "relying on," for the Lord.

chapters.title: Two by Two
chapters.html:
Sirach 33

1No evil will meet the one who fears the Lord;
but in testing he will be rescued again.

2A wise man will not hate the law,
but one who is a hypocrite about it is like a boat in a storm.

3A man of understanding will trust in the law,
and the law is as trustworthy to him as the inquiry of the righteous.

4Prepare what you will say, and so you will be heard;
bind your learning together, and then answer.

5The heart of a fool is like a cartwheel,
and his reasoning like a turning axle.

6A stallion at stud is like a mocking friend:
he neighs under every rider.

7Why is one day better than another,
when all the daylight of the year is from the sun?

8By the Lord's knowledge they were made distinct,
and He made the seasons and feasts different.

9Some of them He exalted and set apart,
and some of them He counted among the ordinary days.

10All men too are from the ground,
and Adam was created out of earth.

11In the fullness of His knowledge the Lord made them distinct,
and made their ways different.

12Some of them He blessed and exalted,
and some He set apart and brought near to Himself;
some He cursed and brought low,
and turned them out of their place.

13Like clay in the potter's hand,
all its ways as he pleases,
so are men in the hand of Him who made them,
to repay them as He judges.

14Good is set against evil,
and life against death;
so the sinner is set against the godly.

15Look in this way at all the works of the Most High:
two by two, one against the other.

16I was the last to keep watch,
like one gleaning after the grape pickers;
by the blessing of the Lord I came in ahead,
and like a grape picker I filled my winepress.

17Consider that I have not labored for myself alone,
but for all who seek discipline.

18Listen to me, you great men of the people,
and you leaders of the assembly, give ear.

19To son or wife, to brother or friend,
do not give power over you while you live;
and do not give your property to another,
or you may change your mind and have to ask for it back.

20While you still live and have breath in you,
do not trade yourself away to anyone.

21It is better that your children ask of you
than that you look to the hands of your sons.

22In all your works keep the upper hand;
do not let a blemish mar your honor.

23When the days of your life come to an end,
at the time of your death, distribute your inheritance.

24Fodder and a stick and burdens for a donkey;
bread and discipline and work for a servant.

25Put your servant to work, and you will find rest;
leave his hands idle, and he will look for freedom.

26Yoke and strap will bow the neck,
and for a wicked servant there are racks and tortures.

27Put him to work so that he is not idle,
for idleness has taught much evil.

28Set him to tasks that fit him,
and if he does not obey, make his fetters heavier.

29But do not go to excess with anyone,
and do nothing without justice.

30If you have a servant, let him be as yourself,
because you acquired him with blood.

31If you have a servant, treat him as yourself,
for you need him as you need your own soul.
If you mistreat him and he sets off and runs away,
on which road will you look for him?

Notes

  • vv1–31 — vv1–15 and the first words of v16 are Swete's 36:1–16; the rest of v16 and vv17–31 are his 30:25–40, divided into verses differently (see the note on 30:25).

  • vv2–3 "will not hate the law… will trust in the law, and the law is as trustworthy to him" — enpisteusei nomō, kai ho nomos autō pistos: he trusts the law, and the law keeps faith with him. The chapter before ends on the same word, Whoever trusts the law (32:24). "The inquiry of the righteous" — erōtēma dikaiōn, as Swete prints it: a question put to God and answered.

  • vv7–12 "exalted and set apart… blessed and exalted… set apart" — hēgiasen and eulogēsen, the two verbs of Genesis 2:3, God blessed the seventh day and set it apart. As God set some days above others, He sets some men above others; Adam was created out of earth recalls Genesis 2:7, The LORD God shaped the human of dust from the ground.

  • vv12–13 "Like clay in the potter's hand" — Paul asks the same of the potter and the clay: Does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? (Romans 9:21).

  • vv14–15 "two by two, one against the other" — dyo dyo, hen katenanti tou henos; the thought returns in 42:24, All things are in pairs, one against the other.

  • v16 "I was the last to keep watch… I came in ahead" — eschatos ēgrypnēsa… ephthasa: he came last, a gleaner after the harvest, and yet arrived first and filled the press.

  • v17 "I have not labored for myself alone" — the line he wrote at the end of wisdom's speech (24:34), See that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek her; here, all who seek discipline.

  • vv30–31 "let him be as yourself… treat him as yourself" — hōs sy… hōs seauton, the words of Leviticus 19:34 for the guest: you shall love him as yourself. "With blood" — en haimati ektēsō auton: what he cost you, paid as dearly as blood.

chapters.title: Dreams, and Offerings from Wrong
chapters.html:
Sirach 34

1Empty and false hopes are for a man without understanding,
and dreams give wings to fools.

2Like one who clutches at a shadow and chases the wind
is the one who pays attention to dreams.

3What one sees in dreams is one thing set against another,
the likeness of a face facing a face.

4From what is unclean, what can be made clean?
From what is false, what can come true?

5Divinations and omens and dreams are empty,
and the heart imagines things like a woman in labor.

6Unless they are sent from the Most High as a visitation,
do not give your heart to them.

7Dreams have led many astray,
and those who hoped in them have fallen.

8Without lies the law will be fulfilled,
and wisdom is made complete in a faithful mouth.

9A well-disciplined man knows many things,
and a man of much experience will speak with understanding.

10One who has not been tested knows little,
but one who has wandered will grow in shrewdness.

11I have seen many things in my wanderings,
and I understand more than I can say.

12Often I have been in danger even of death,
and I came through because of these things.

13The spirit of those who fear the Lord will live,
for their hope is in the One who saves them.

14Whoever fears the Lord will not be afraid,
and will not lose heart, for He is his hope.

15Happy is the soul of the one who fears the Lord.
On whom does he lean? Who is his support?

16The eyes of the Lord are on those who love Him,
a mighty shield and a strong support,
a shelter from the scorching wind and a shade from the noonday sun,
a guard against stumbling and a help against falling.

17He lifts up the soul and gives light to the eyes;
He gives healing, life and blessing.

18Whoever sacrifices from what was wrongly gained makes a mockery of an offering,
and the mockeries of the lawless do not win favor.

19The Most High takes no pleasure in the offerings of the ungodly,
nor does He atone for sins for a multitude of sacrifices.

20Like one who sacrifices a son in front of his father
is the one who brings a sacrifice from the property of the poor.

21The bread of the needy is the life of the poor;
whoever robs them of it is a man of blood.

22To take away a neighbor's living is to murder him,
and to rob a hired man of his wages is to shed blood.

23One builds and another tears down;
what do they gain but toil?

24One prays and another curses;
whose voice will the Master hear?

25One who is washed after touching a dead body and touches it again,
what has he gained by his washing?

26So it is with a man who fasts for his sins,
and goes again and does the same:
who will listen to his prayer?
What has he gained by humbling himself?

Notes

  • vv1–26 — Swete's 31:1–31. The English joins five pairs of his verses into one (here vv10, 13, 15, 18 and 22); see the note on 30:25.

  • vv1–8 "Divinations and omens and dreams are empty" — manteiai kai oiōnismoi, the words of the Greek of Deuteronomy 18:10, one who reads omens, one who practices divination. One door is left open: unless they are sent from the Most High (v6), as the LORD said, I speak with him in a dream (Numbers 12:6).

  • v3 "the likeness of a face facing a face" — katenanti prosōpou homoiōma prosōpou: a dream is a mirror, and the dreamer sees his own face looking back.

  • vv9–10 "A well-disciplined man… one who has wandered" — pepaideumenos and peplanēmenos, two words a few letters apart: the man trained at home and the man taught by the road. The writer claims both (vv11–12).

  • v16 "The eyes of the Lord are on those who love Him" — Psalm 33:18, The eye of the LORD is on those who fear Him, and in its Greek the same words, hoi ophthalmoi Kyriou epi. "A shade from the noonday sun" — Psalm 121:5–6, the LORD is your shade… The sun will not strike you by day.

  • v18 "makes a mockery of an offering… the mockeries of the lawless" — memōkēmenē, mōkēmata: the same word twice. Proverbs 21:27, The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable.

  • v20 "Like one who sacrifices a son in front of his father" — thyōn, the verb of the altar: a gift taken from the poor is offered up to God as though their own child were the victim.

  • vv21–22 "to rob a hired man of his wages is to shed blood" — Leviticus 19:13, The wages of a hired man shall not stay with you overnight until morning; Deuteronomy 24:15, Otherwise he will cry to the LORD against you.

  • v25 "One who is washed after touching a dead body" — the cleansing of Numbers 19:11–12. Baptizomenos, "washed," is the verb of John's baptism in the Jordan (Matthew 3:6); here it is the old washing from a corpse, undone by touching it again.

chapters.title: The Offering the Lord Accepts
chapters.html:
Sirach 35

1Whoever keeps the law makes many offerings;
whoever pays attention to the commandments sacrifices a peace offering.

2Whoever repays a kindness offers fine flour,
and whoever gives charity sacrifices a thank offering.

3To turn away from evil is what pleases the Lord,
and to turn away from injustice is atonement.

4Do not appear before the Lord empty-handed,

5for all these things are done because of the commandment.

6The offering of the righteous enriches the altar,
and its fragrance is before the Most High.

7The sacrifice of a righteous man is acceptable,
and its memorial will not be forgotten.

8Glorify the Lord with a good eye,
and do not stint the firstfruits of your hands.

9In every gift show a cheerful face,
and set apart your tithe with gladness.

10Give to the Most High as He has given to you,
and with a good eye, as much as your hand has found.

11For the Lord is One who repays,
and He will repay you sevenfold.

12Do not offer bribes, for He will not accept them,
and do not rely on an unjust sacrifice;
for the Lord is the judge,
and with Him there is no partiality.

13He will not show partiality against a poor man,
and He will listen to the prayer of one who is wronged.

14He will not ignore the plea of the orphan,
or the widow when she pours out her complaint.

15Do not a widow's tears run down her cheek,
and is not her cry against the one who made them fall?

16Whoever serves willingly will be accepted,
and his prayer will reach the clouds.

17The prayer of the humble passes through the clouds,

chapters.title: Have Mercy on Us
chapters.html:
Sirach 36

1Have mercy on us, Master, God of all,
and look upon us,

2and send the fear of You on all the nations.

3Lift up Your hand against foreign nations,
and let them see Your might.

4As before their eyes You have shown Yourself holy among us,
so before our eyes show Yourself great among them;

5let them know You, as we too have known You,
that there is no God but You, Lord.

6Renew signs and work other wonders;
glorify Your hand and Your right arm.

7Rouse anger and pour out wrath;
remove the adversary and wipe out the enemy.

8Hasten the time and remember the oath,
and let them tell of Your mighty deeds.

9In fiery wrath let whoever escapes be consumed,
and may those who harm Your people find destruction.

10Crush the heads of the enemy rulers,
who say, "There is no one but us."

11Gather all the tribes of Jacob,
and give them their inheritance as at the beginning.

12Have mercy, Lord, on the people called by Your name,
on Israel, whom You likened to a firstborn.

13Have pity on the city of Your sanctuary,
Jerusalem, the city of Your rest.

14Fill Zion with the telling of Your mighty deeds,
and Your people with Your glory.

15Bear witness to those You created in the beginning,
and bring to pass the prophecies spoken in Your name.

16Reward those who wait for You,
and let Your prophets be found trustworthy.

17Hear, Lord, the prayer of those who plead with You,
according to Aaron's blessing over Your people,
and all who are on the earth will know
that You are the Lord, the God of the ages.

18The stomach will eat any food,
yet one food is better than another.

19As the palate tastes game,
so an understanding heart tastes lying words.

20A crooked heart causes grief,
but a man of experience will pay him back.

21A woman will accept any man,
but one daughter is better than another.

22A woman's beauty brightens the face,
and surpasses every desire of a man.

23If there is mercy and gentleness on her tongue,
her husband is not like other men.

24Whoever gains a wife makes a beginning of possessions,
a helper fit for him and a pillar to rest on.

25Where there is no fence, property is plundered,
and where there is no wife, a man wanders and groans.

26Who will trust a nimble robber
who darts from city to city?
So it is with a man who has no nest,
and lodges wherever night overtakes him.

Notes

  • vv1–26 — vv1–10 and the first words of v11 are Swete's 33:1–13, divided into verses differently; the rest of v11 is the end of his 36:16, and vv12–26 are his 36:17–31 (see the note on 30:25).

  • v4 "As before their eyes You have shown Yourself holy among us" — enōpion autōn hēgiasthēs en hēmin, the words of God's promise in the Greek of Ezekiel 36:23, when I am shown holy among you before their eyes. The prayer asks Him to do among the nations what He has done among Israel.

  • vv5, 10 "there is no God but You… There is no one but us" — ouk estin theos plēn sou… ouk estin plēn hēmōn: the rulers' boast is the confession of v5 turned on themselves.

  • v6 "glorify Your hand and Your right arm" — Exodus 15:6, Your right hand, LORD, is majestic in power, where the Greek has the same verb, dedoxastai, "is glorified."

  • v12 "whom You likened to a firstborn" — Exodus 4:22, Israel is My son, My firstborn. "The city of Your rest" (v13) — Psalm 132:14, This is My resting place forever.

  • v17 "according to Aaron's blessing over Your people" — the blessing of Numbers 6:24–27, which ends, So they shall put My name on the sons of Israel, and I will bless them; the prayer asks God to keep His own blessing.

  • v19 "As the palate tastes game, so an understanding heart tastes lying words" — Job 12:11, Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes its food?

  • v24 "a helper fit for him" — boēthon kat' auton, the words of the Greek of Genesis 2:18, where the Hebrew is a help as his counterpart. "A man who has no nest" (v26) — Reproof 3:8 (Proverbs 27:8), Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home.

chapters.title: Friends and Counselors
chapters.html:
Sirach 37

1Every friend will say, "I too am his friend,"
but there is a friend who is a friend in name only.

2Is it not a grief close to death
when a companion and friend turns into an enemy?

3O wicked thought, where did you roll in from,
to cover the dry land with deceit?

4A companion delights in a friend's gladness,
but in a time of trouble he will be against him.

5A companion toils with a friend for the sake of his belly,
and in the face of battle he will take up the shield.

6Do not forget a friend in your soul,
and do not be unmindful of him in your wealth.

7Every counselor praises his own counsel,
but there is one who counsels for his own sake.

8Guard yourself against a counselor,
and first find out what he needs,
for he will take counsel for himself;
he may cast the lot over you,

9and say to you, "Your way is good,"
and then stand off to see what will happen to you.

10Do not consult one who looks at you with suspicion,
and hide your counsel from those who envy you.

11With a woman about her rival, with a coward about war,
with a merchant about trade, with a buyer about selling,
with a grudging man about gratitude,
with a merciless man about kindness,
with a lazy man about any work,
with a hired man far from home about finishing the job,
with an idle servant about much work —
do not rely on these for any counsel.

12But stay close to a godly man,
whom you know to keep the commandments,
whose soul is like your own soul,
and who will grieve with you if you stumble.

13Hold fast to the counsel of your own heart,
for no one is more trustworthy to you than it.

14A man's soul sometimes tells him more
than seven watchmen sitting high on a watchtower.

15Above all this, pray to the Most High
that He may direct your way in truth.

16Reason is the beginning of every work,
and counsel comes before every action.

17A change of heart leaves its track:

18four things spring up, good and evil, life and death,
and what rules over them continually is the tongue.

19There is a shrewd man who teaches many,
and is useless to himself.

20There is one who plays the wise man in words and is hated;
he will end up lacking all food,

21for grace has not been given him from the Lord,
because he has been stripped of all wisdom.

22There is one who is wise for his own soul,
and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy on his lips.

23A wise man will teach his own people,
and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy.

24A wise man will be filled with blessing,
and all who see him will call him happy.

25A man's life is counted in days,
but the days of Israel are without number.

26The wise man will inherit trust among his people,
and his name will live forever.

27My child, test your soul while you live;
see what is bad for it, and do not give it that.

28For not everything is good for everyone,
and not every soul takes pleasure in everything.

29Do not be greedy for every delicacy,
and do not throw yourself upon the food;

30for with much eating comes sickness,
and greed will bring on vomiting.

31Through greed many have died,
but whoever takes care will add to his life.

Notes

  • v2 "a grief close to death" — lypē… heōs thanatou. In Gethsemane, on the night a friend betrayed Him, Jesus says, My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death (Matthew 26:38), in the same Greek words, perilypos… heōs thanatou.

  • v8 "he may cast the lot over you" — balē epi soi klēron: he treats you as spoil to be divided, as in Psalm 22:18, for my clothing they cast lots (Greek ebalon klēron).

  • v11 "With a woman about her rival" — the rival wife of 26:6; each person in the list is the one with the most to gain from bad advice on that very matter.

  • v11 "a hired man far from home" — misthiou aphestiou, as Swete prints it, "a hired man without a hearth": a man with no stake in the place, who will not see the job through.

  • vv13–14 "Hold fast to the counsel of your own heart… more than seven watchmen" — after every outside counselor has been weighed, the heart is the most trustworthy, pistoteros; and above it, prayer (v15).

  • vv17–18 "good and evil, life and death… the tongue" — the choice of Deuteronomy 30:15, I have set before you today life and good, and death and evil, and the power Proverbs gives the tongue, Death and life are in the power of the tongue (18:21).

  • v28 "For not everything is good for everyone" — ou panta pasin sympherei. Paul uses the same verb: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial (ou panta sympherei, 1 Corinthians 6:12).

  • vv29–31 — the warning of the great table in 31:12–21 again: greed at food ends in vomiting, the same word, cholera.

chapters.title: The Physician, the Dead, and the Trades
chapters.html:
Sirach 38

1Honor the physician with the honor due him for your needs,
for the Lord created him too.

2For healing comes from the Most High,
and he will receive a gift from the king.

3The physician's skill will lift up his head,
and he will be admired in the presence of great men.

4The Lord created medicines out of the earth,
and a sensible man will not despise them.

5Was not water made sweet by wood,
so that its power might be known?

6He gave skill to men,
so that He might be glorified in His wonders.

7With them He heals and takes away pain;

8the apothecary makes a mixture from them.
His works will never come to an end,
and from Him well-being is over the face of the earth.

9My child, when you are ill, do not neglect it,
but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you.

10Put away your wrongdoing and make your hands straight,
and cleanse your heart from all sin.

11Offer a fragrant offering and a memorial of fine flour,
and make your offering rich, as one who will soon be no more.

12Then give the physician his place, for the Lord created him too;
do not let him leave you, for you need him.

13There is a time when success lies in their hands too,

14for they too will pray to the Lord
to grant them success in bringing relief
and healing, to preserve life.

15Whoever sins before his Maker,
may he fall into the hands of the physician.

16My child, let your tears fall over the dead,
and begin the lament as one who suffers terribly;
wrap his body as is his due,
and do not neglect his burial.

17Make the weeping bitter and the mourning warm,
and keep the mourning as he deserves,
a day or two, to avoid reproach;
then be comforted for your grief's sake.

18For grief leads to death,
and grief of heart saps strength.

19When he is carried away, grief too passes;
a poor man's life is against the heart.

20Do not give your heart over to grief;
drive it away, remembering your own end.

21Do not forget: there is no coming back;
you will do him no good, and you will harm yourself.

22Remember that his sentence will also be yours:
"Yesterday for me, and today for you."

23When the dead is at rest, let his memory rest,
and be comforted for him when his spirit has gone out.

24The wisdom of the scribe comes through the opportunity of leisure,
and whoever has little business will become wise.

25How can he become wise who holds the plow
and boasts in the shaft of the goad,
who drives oxen and is busy with their labors,
and whose talk is about bullocks?

26He sets his heart on turning furrows,
and he lies awake over fodder for the heifers.

27So it is with every craftsman and master builder,
who works by night as by day;
those who engrave seals,
whose patience goes into varying the design:
he sets his heart on making the likeness true,
and he lies awake to finish the work.

28So it is with the smith sitting by the anvil,
intent on the iron he works;
the breath of the fire withers his flesh,
and he struggles with the heat of the furnace;
the sound of the hammer is always new in his ear,
and his eyes are on the pattern of the vessel;
he sets his heart on finishing his works,
and he lies awake to adorn them at the end.

29So it is with the potter sitting at his work
and turning the wheel with his feet,
always anxious over his work,
and all he makes is counted;

30with his arm he shapes the clay,
and with his feet he bends its strength;
he sets his heart on finishing the glaze,
and he lies awake to clean the kiln.

31All these rely on their hands,
and each is wise in his own work.

32Without them no city can be built,
and no one could live there as a guest or walk its streets.

33In the assembly they do not rise to the top,
and they do not ponder the covenant of judgment;
they do not sit on the judge's seat,
nor do they declare righteousness and judgment,
and they are not found among the makers of proverbs.

34But they keep the fabric of the world standing,
and their prayer is in the work of their craft.

Notes

  • vv1–15 "the Lord created him too" — the physician and his medicines are both the Lord's making (vv1, 4, 12). The order is prayer first (v9), then the physician (v12); compare King Asa, who even in his disease did not seek the LORD, but the healers (2 Chronicles 16:12).

  • v5 "Was not water made sweet by wood" — apo xylou, the tree Moses threw into the bitter water at Marah (Exodus 15:25, where the Greek too has xylon): a medicine out of the earth, given by the Lord.

  • vv6–8 "He gave skill… With them He heals… His works will never come to an end" — the Greek does not name who heals or whose works go on; v6, He gave skill to men, is the Lord, and the lines that follow are read the same way: He heals through the remedies the apothecary mixes.

  • v11 "a fragrant offering and a memorial of fine flour" — euōdian kai mnēmosynon semidaleōs, the words of the grain offering (Leviticus 2:2) met in 35:6–7. "As one who will soon be no more" — hōs mē hyparchōn, "as not existing."

  • v15 "may he fall into the hands of the physician" — empesoi, a wish: either sickness is the sinner's due, or the sinner too must be sent to the physician. The Greek leaves both.

  • v19 "When he is carried away, grief too passes" — en apagōgē parabainei kai lypē: apagōgē is a "leading away"; read here as the dead carried out for burial. The second line, a poor man's life is against the heart, is as compressed in the Greek.

  • v22 "Yesterday for me, and today for you" — the dead man speaks: what was his sentence yesterday is yours today (Genesis 3:19, to dust you shall return).

  • vv24–34 "The wisdom of the scribe" — the farmer, the engraver, the smith and the potter, each with the same refrain, he sets his heart… he lies awake (vv26, 27, 28, 30), are praised and then set below the scribe, who has leisure to become wise (39:1–11). Yet their prayer is in the work of their craft (v34).

  • v28 "the sound of the hammer is always new in his ear" — kainiei to ous autou, "will make his ear new," as Swete prints it: the blow that never stops sounding.

chapters.title: The Scribe, and the Works of the Lord
chapters.html:
Sirach 39

1Not so the one who devotes his soul
and ponders the law of the Most High:
he will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients,
and be occupied with prophecies;

2he will keep the stories of famous men,
and enter into the twists of parables;

3he will seek out the hidden things of proverbs,
and spend his time among the riddles of parables.

4He will serve among great men,
and appear before a ruler;
he will travel through the land of foreign nations,
for he has tested good and evil among men.

5He will set his heart to rise early
to the Lord who made him,
and will plead before the Most High;
he will open his mouth in prayer,
and plead for his sins.

6If the great Lord wills,
he will be filled with a spirit of understanding;
he will rain down words of wisdom,
and give thanks to the Lord in prayer.

7He will direct his counsel and knowledge,
and ponder His hidden things.

8He will bring to light the discipline he teaches,
and will boast in the law of the Lord's covenant.

9Many will praise his understanding;
it will never be blotted out;
his memory will not depart,
and his name will live from generation to generation.

10Nations will tell of his wisdom,
and the assembly will proclaim his praise.

11If he lives long, he will leave a name greater than a thousand;
and if he goes to his rest, it is enough for him.

12Once more I will set out what I have pondered,
for I am full like the moon at mid-month.

13Listen to me, holy sons,
and blossom like a rose growing by a stream in the field;

14send out fragrance like frankincense,
and blossom like a lily;
spread fragrance and sing a song of praise;
bless the Lord for all His works.

15Ascribe greatness to His name,
and give thanks with His praise,
with songs on your lips and with harps;
and this is what you shall say in giving thanks:

16All the works of the Lord are very good,
and every command of His will be done in its time.

17No one can say, "What is this? Why is that?"
for everything will be sought out in its time.
At His word the water stood like a heap,
and at the word of His mouth, the storehouses of water.

18At His command is all His good pleasure,
and no one can lessen His salvation.

19The works of all flesh are before Him,
and nothing can be hidden from His eyes.

20From everlasting to everlasting He looks,
and nothing is too wonderful for Him.

21No one can say, "What is this? Why is that?"
for everything has been created for its own use.

22His blessing covers like a river,
and like a flood it drenches the dry land.

23So the nations will inherit His wrath,
as He turned waters into salt.

24His ways are straight for the holy;
so they are stumbling blocks for the lawless.

25Good things were created for the good from the beginning;
so evil things for sinners.

26The first needs of man's life
are water and fire and iron and salt,
fine wheat flour and honey and milk,
the blood of the grape, and oil and clothing.

27All these are for good to the godly;
so for sinners they will be turned to evil.

28There are winds created for vengeance,
and in their fury they make their scourges firm;
in the time of the end they will pour out their strength,
and calm the anger of Him who made them.

29Fire and hail, famine and death,
all these were created for vengeance;

30the teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions and vipers,
and the sword that takes vengeance on the ungodly to destroy them.

31They will rejoice in His command,
and be made ready on earth for their uses,
and in their seasons they will not disobey His word.

32Therefore from the beginning I was resolved,
and I pondered, and I left it in writing:

33All the works of the Lord are good,
and He will supply every need in its hour.

34No one can say, "This is worse than that,"
for everything will prove good in its season.

35So now with all the heart and with the mouth we have sung praise;
bless the name of the Lord.

Notes

  • v1 "ponders the law of the Most High" — the man of Psalm 1:2, on His law he meditates day and night. Against the farmer and the craftsmen of 38:25–34, the scribe devotes his soul.

  • v3 "the riddles of parables" — what Proverbs sets out to teach, to understand a proverb and a figure, the words of the wise and their riddles (1:6).

  • v5 "He will set his heart" — tēn kardian autou epidōsei, the craftsmen's refrain in 38:26–30 (kardian autou dōsei, kardian epidōsei). They set their hearts on furrows, seals, iron and clay; he sets his heart on rising early to the Lord.

  • v15 "Ascribe greatness to His name" — dote… megalōsynēn, the call of the Song of Moses, ascribe greatness to our God! (Deuteronomy 32:3), in the same Greek words.

  • v16 "All the works of the Lord are very good… in its time" — Genesis 1:31, it was very good; Ecclesiastes 3:11, He has made everything beautiful in its time.

  • vv17, 21, 34 "No one can say" — three times the hymn shuts the mouth of the one who questions a part of creation, and three times gives the reason: its time, its use, its season.

  • v17 "the water stood like a heap… the storehouses of water" — the sea at the crossing, where the waters were heaped up (Exodus 15:8), and Psalm 33:7, He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; He puts the deeps in storehouses.

  • v23 "as He turned waters into salt" — eis halmēn, the word of Psalm 107:34 in Greek, a fruitful land into a salt waste, because of the wickedness of those who live there.

  • v28 "There are winds created for vengeance" — pneumata, "winds" or "spirits": the list that follows (fire, hail, famine, death, beasts, the sword) reads as forces of nature sent by God. "The teeth of wild beasts" (v30) — Deuteronomy 32:24, the teeth of beasts I will send against them.
